transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Jamal Ortega (Redwood PSM); Linh Tran (CTO, Sapphire), Marco Ruiz (Platform Eng), Dina Kaur (SRE)

Summary (auto):
Deep technical session to validate autoscale/reserve tradeoffs for Sapphire's genAI product. Focus on adaptive reserved pools, prewarm windows, queueing behavior under long-tail traffic, KV cache warmup impact, and VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployments.

Topics: adaptive-reserve, prewarm, burst throttling, k/v cache warmup, continuous batching, quantization memory, VPC egress, encryption/KMS, SOC2

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan (AE): okay hi everyone thanks for hopping on, uh quick intros, um i'm Evan from Redwood, AE, and with me Priya and Jamal.
[00:18] Linh (CTO): hey thanks Evan, I'm Linh, CTO at Sapphire. We have Marco and Dina on the call. We want to focus on capacity planning — mostly burst and reserved behaviour for our inference pipeline.
[00:33] Priya (SE): Great, thanks. Quick agenda: we'll run through current traffic, show an adaptive-reserve pattern we've run internally, then dig into kv cache warmup and batching impacts, and end with pricing/next steps.
[00:46] Marco: sounds good. We sent sample traffic last night but didn't include run-of-week bursts. Expect some 10x spikes for less than 2 minutes.
[00:58] Dina: also FYI we run private deployment in a VPC, we need KMS integration and audit logs. SOC 2 stuff is critical for compliance.
[01:12] Priya: noted, we'll cover KMS and audit pointers later, jamal will follow up on security pack.
[01:20] Priya: okay first, can you confirm model sizes and typical sequence lengths?
[01:26] Marco: model is a 13B opt variant, quantized to 4-bit roughly, token distribution 8-512 but p95 around 220.
[01:36] Evan: perfect — those numbers drive kernel choices and KV cache behavior.
[01:42] [00:60] Speaker 1: (mumble) so the KV cash warming — is that prefix cache?
[02:05] Priya: yeah we mean prefix and KV cache (sometimes folks say k/v kache), we use a two-tier caching: local GPU ephemeral cache + shared coldstore for prewarmed states. For burst we recommend prewarm windows and adaptive reserved slabs.
[02:25] Linh: how does Redwood decide to scale reserved GPUs vs burst into ephemeral pool? we want to avoid overprovisioning cost but also keep the tail latencies acceptable.
[02:36] Priya: good question. We run a queueing model that treats reserved pool as high-priority servers and ephemeral (burst) as lower priority with higher cold-start cost. We simulate using arrival distributions — Weibull for tails — and set target p99 latency SLO. The control loop uses a rolling-window estimator to grow reserved capacity when sustained exceedance occurs, but allows short spikes to be absorbed by prewarmed ephemeral instances (if prewarm credits available).
[03:04] Marco: can you show the math?
[03:08] Priya: sure, simplified: we model latency L as service time + queue wait. Service time depends on batch size and quantization; quant 4-bit had 20-30% lower mem and slight CPU decode overhead. For queueing we approximate M/G/k but with nonstationary arrivals so we use simulation — we fed your traffic histograms and observed tail amplification with a small reserved pool.
[03:39] Dina: by tail amplification you mean p99 jumps when a few large requests arrive and evict KV cache?
[03:45] Priya: Exactly. We saw cases where large seq lengths cause KV cache thrash, warmed KV entries are evicted, subsequent requests pay cache miss plus token decode for prefix. That adds 200-800ms in our internal runs.
[03:59] Evan: this is where prewarm helps: keep N prewarmed slots pinned with KV snapshot so short bursts hit warmed state. But that costs reserved GPU hours.
[04:12] Linh: what's the suggested ratio of prewarm slots to baseline reserved capacity?
[04:16] Priya: it depends on burst shape; rule-of-thumb: for short 1-3 minute spikes, prewarm slots covering 15-25% of expected peak QPS reduces p99 by ~40% in our sim. For longer sustained spikes, better to scale reserved capacity.
[04:33] Marco: what's Redwood's prewarm warmup time for a 13B quant model?
[04:37] Priya: around 30-90 seconds for full KV population depending on sequence distribution; with kv snapshot restore (we store a compacted prefix snapshot) it can be <12s in many cases. But snapshot restore requires dedicated memory and indexing, otherwise cold load is tens of seconds.
[04:57] [05:00] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) hmm okay
[05:06] Priya: on batching — continuous batching helps amortize kernel launches, but increases tail for single-user low-latency requests. Our runtime supports latency-aware batching: small headroom windows and dynamic batch cutoffs.
[05:20] Marco: can we see tradeoffs?
[05:23] Priya: yes, slide shown — at 4ms headroom batching we reduce token cost ~28% at 95th pct but p95 latency grows 12%. With priority queueing you can have critical routes with minimal batching and background routes with aggressive batching.
[05:40] Linh: VPC/on-prem constraints — if we run Private in our VPC, do we still get prewarm snapshot sync?
[05:48] Priya: yes. Private deployment offers the same control plane for orchestration; snapshots are stored in your S3 or internal object store and restored within your network. KMS must be provided for key wrapping; we integrate with AWS KMS/GCP KMS/HSMs.
[06:04] Dina: how about network egress and tensor offloads? we have strict egress policies, can't call public endpoints.
[06:10] Jamal (PSM): that's common, we can operate fully air-gapped; the control plane connection can be private or eliminated for on-prem. The runtime and orchestration live inside your VPC.
[06:21] Priya: a key operational lever is adaptive reserve: we cap a baseline reserved slab sized for average sustained load and configure an adaptive controller that scales by discrete slab increments when 5-min rolling p95>target. We add backoff so it doesn't oscillate.
[06:38] Marco: what's the minimum slab size? one GPU? or fractional?
[06:42] Priya: managed at GPU-level; we recommend slab increments of 1-2 GPUs for 13B depending on your throughput. Redwood Dedicated can also offer fractional slices for specific SKUs but there's complexity around noisy neighbor. We can discuss fractional later.
[06:58] Linh: cost modeling — can you show cost-per-token vs latency curves?
[07:03] Priya: yes for your workload we estimated active cost: reserved-only was cheaper at high sustained load; for bursty patterns a hybrid reserve+burst with prewarm credits saved ~22% on expected monthly spend vs pure-overprovision.
[07:20] Evan: important nuance — quantization also reduces RAM so you fit more instances per GPU, but beam/search patterns and kv cache size matter.
[07:30] Marco: you mentioned 'kv snapshot' — how often do you persist snapshots?
[07:34] Priya: snapshots are incremental; by default we checkpoint after model boot + every X minutes, configurable. For low-latency we recommend keeping recent prefixes for 10-30 minutes for common prompts. That trades off storage and restore times.
[07:51] [08:00] Speaker 3: (background) 
[08:06] Dina: security question — audit logs and key management for private: are logs stored in customer S3 or sent to Redwood?
[08:13] Jamal: logs can be kept entirely in-customer S3 with optional forwarding; we also offer hashed audit streams to Redwood's control plane for support, only if customer opts in. Everything can be KMS-wrapped.
[08:26] Linh: okay good. Also, provider lock-in — if we move to other runtime later, can we export snapshots?
[08:34] Priya: snapshots are portable in a supported format; you get metadata and the compaction format. Some low-level tuning is runtime-specific but we can export and document.
[08:44] Marco: curious about backpressure — how does Redwood handle queue blowouts during sustained 10x spikes?
[08:50] Priya: we have multi-tier policies: soft-throttle at ingress (reject or enqueue with TTL), priority lanes, and graceful degradation fallback to a smaller cheaper model variant. Fallbacks can be configured per-route.
[09:05] Linh: we need to keep degradation predictably graceful — for our customers p95 is more important than absolute throughput during incidents.
[09:12] Priya: then we'd set route-level SLOs and a priority queue: critical routes have reserved slots and low batching; background ones batch aggressively and can be dropped if needed.
[09:23] Marco: any real-world numbers on p99 improvements with the adaptive reserve algorithm?
[09:28] Priya: in a sample with heavy long-tail from one of our retail customers we reduced p99 by ~45% after adding small prewarm slots covering 20% peak and tuning eviction thresholds.
[09:40] Evan: also note cache eviction policy matters — we use LRU with hot-key pinning for common prefixes to avoid churn.
[09:49] Dina: what's the operational cost to maintain snapshots? does it add IOPS on storage?
[09:54] Priya: depends on checkpoint freq and object store; incremental checkpoints are small but restoration IO happens at boot. We recommend using local NVMe for fastest restore.
[10:05] Marco: question on quantization and kernel selection — if we use 4-bit quant + mixed kernels, do you see any latency regression?
[10:12] Priya: sometimes for generation-heavy workloads there is slight decode CPU overhead but GPU kernel throughput is higher. Net latency is often improved but depends on per-token compute pattern. We run microbenchmarks per-customer.
[10:28] [11:00] Speaker 1: (uh)
[11:06] Linh: can you recap the main knobs we should tune?
[11:09] Priya: baseline reserved slab, prewarm slots (KV snapshot count), batch headroom, priority lanes, adaptive scaling thresholds and backoff, fallback smaller model variants, and checkpoint frequency.
[11:25] Marco: for our immediate pilot what do you recommend?
[11:28] Priya: start with a small reserved slab sized for 50% of peak, enable 15% prewarm slots, shallow batching (low headroom), and configure adaptive scaling with 5-min windows. We'll run a simulated 14-day replay using your histograms.
[11:44] Evan: we'll also run a short in-staging benchmark to validate cold vs warm restores and p95/p99 under synthetic burst traffic.
[11:54] Linh: great. About pricing for reserved — we'd like a slab pricing with prewarm credit included for first 30 days.
[12:01] Evan: noted, i'll include prewarm credit option in the pricing.
[12:06] Marco: security follow-up, jamal will you own the SOC2 docs handoff?
[12:10] Jamal: yes, i'll send the security pack and a checklist for KMS/HSM integration.
[12:14] [12:30] Speaker 2: (mumble)
[12:36] Priya: a few gotchas — one is fractional GPU packing: while cost saving, fractional can increase cold-start variance because packing/unpacking moves tensors around. For predictable SLOs we often prefer whole-GPU slabs.
[12:55] Linh: noted. Also, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[12:59] Priya: ideally: per-request size, seq len, model id, route, outcome (success/error), timestamps, and KV cache hit/miss if you can instrument. That allows our sim to be accurate.
[13:14] Marco: we'll try to provide those fields.
[13:18] Evan: quick pause — any regulatory constraints about snapshot persistence?
[13:22] Dina: snapshots must stay in region X and be encrypted with our KMS.
[13:27] Priya: that's fine, snapshots stored in-customer S3 in-region and encrypted.
[13:33] [14:00] Speaker 4: (background notification sound)
[14:06] Linh: can you put together a recommended config for our pilot?
[14:09] Priya: yes we'll deliver a config doc: reserved slab size, prewarm count, adaptive thresholds, batching policy, and rollback/fallback rules.
[14:18] Priya: rough timeline: we'll run simulation (Priya) by 5/17, pricing and POC contract (Evan) by 5/12, security pack (Jamal) by 5/13, and staging benchmark wk of 5/18.
[14:34] Marco: perfect. Any blockers from Redwood side to run staging inside our VPC?
[14:38] Jamal: none, we'll coordinate network and IAM details; we might need a short on-call window for the benchmark.
[14:46] Linh: sounds good.
[14:48] Evan: okay let's do quick recap and close.
[14:52] Recap:
- Redwood will run a 14-day traffic replay and queueing sim using supplied histograms (Priya).
- Redwood to propose reserved slab + prewarm credits pricing and contract draft (Evan).
- Security pack and KMS/HSM notes (Jamal).
- Sapphire to share detailed histograms and retention/region constraints (Linh).

1) Priya uploads sim results and config doc (by 2026-05-17).

[15:40] Linh: thanks everyone, appreciate the concrete plan.
[15:44] Evan: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and artifacts.
[15:48] Marco: thanks.
[15:50] Dina: bye.
